Sorting Algorithms

AlgorithmsPermutationsCounting
Game: Watch five different ways of putting a row of numbers in order, from smallest to largest, and see which is quickest.
How to play: Pick a method and press Run, or One step to go slowly. Tick Same array to race the methods on the same numbers.

Look for the math

A sorting algorithm puts a list in order using only two moves: compare two entries, and swap them. Methods differ in which pairs they compare, and so in how many comparisons and swaps they need. Here one step is one comparison.

Swaps and inversions

An inversion is a pair of entries in the wrong order. Swapping two neighbours that are out of order removes exactly one inversion, so insertion sort and bubblesort each make exactly as many swaps as the array has inversions: none for Ascending, n(n−1)/2 for Descending. The logic test confirmed this on hundreds of random arrays.

Counting comparisons

As written here (after the applet), the inner loops never stop early, so insertion sort and bubblesort always take n(n−1)/2 steps, and selection sort n(n+1)/2, however the numbers start. That grows like n²: twice the size, four times the work. Shellsort first sorts entries 13 or 4 apart, so that far-flung entries travel in a few long jumps. Heapsort arranges the array as a heap (every entry at least as big as its two children), then repeatedly moves the top to the end. Here each of its steps is a whole sift, so it needs about 3n/2 steps, though each one does more work.

Two repairs

Two of the applet's methods misbehave. Its bubblesort never announces that it has finished. Its heapsort, copied from code that counts places from 1, never touches the first entry, and so often leaves the array unsorted. The test checked both against a copy of the applet's code. This page mends them; the other three methods are the applet's own, step for step.

Tick Same array, then run every method on Descending numbers. Which makes the most swaps, and which the fewest?
